inputs.need:
I am a surveillance epidemiologist at a regional public health agency serving about 2.4 million people. Our syndromic surveillance system scans emergency department chief complaints and pharmacy sales every morning and generates about 35 statistical alerts a week for respiratory, gastrointestinal and rash syndromes. Each alert is validated by the epidemiologist on duty, who looks at line lists, calls hospitals if needed and decides whether to escalate. We have no written procedure: some of us spend two hours on an alert and others dismiss it in five minutes, and last winter a norovirus cluster in two care homes was dismissed twice before the third alert was escalated.

We have drafted a structured validation checklist with fixed data checks (duplicate records, reporting artefacts, clustering by age and place, comparison with laboratory reports) and a rule for when to escalate. I am not sure how to evaluate it. One option is to treat it like a test and estimate its sensitivity and specificity against a panel review of past alerts. Another is to randomise incoming alerts, or duty days, to the checklist or to usual validation for six months and compare the time to a validation decision and the events that were missed. My director wants to know whether the checklist makes validation faster without missing real events before it becomes standard procedure.

Six epidemiologists share the duty rota and we cannot hire. Alerts and decisions are logged in our surveillance database with time stamps, and outbreak reports from laboratories and local health units tell us later which alerts were real. The chair of the agency's research ethics committee has confirmed that an evaluation of an internal procedure that uses no personal information counts as program evaluation.
inputs.constraints: No new staff; six epidemiologists on the duty rota; a six-month evaluation from January to June 2027; alert logs and later outbreak reports are the only data sources.

response.subtitle: Design not yet settled: accuracy study or randomised comparison of validation procedures
response.statement: About 35 syndromic surveillance alerts a week are validated by the epidemiologist on duty without a written procedure, with large differences in time spent and at least one recent cluster dismissed twice before escalation. records.title: Structured versus usual validation of syndromic surveillance alerts: a randomised comparison in a regional public health unit
records.authors: Lindqvist-Achebe M, Osei-Carvalho R, Brandt-Nakamura E
records.abstract: Over 20 weeks, 412 syndromic surveillance alerts in one regional public health unit were randomised individually to a structured validation protocol or to usual review by the epidemiologist on duty. Randomising alerts to a structured protocol shortened the median time to a validation decision from 96 to 42 minutes. Escalations were similar (6 against 7 per 100 alerts). Two true events were dismissed at the first alert in the protocol arm and three in the usual arm, too few to compare. Epidemiologists reported applying parts of the protocol to usual-review alerts after the first month, which may have reduced the difference.

records.title: Positive predictive value of syndromic surveillance alerts for confirmed outbreaks: a five-year review
records.abstract: We linked 8,900 alerts from a syndromic surveillance system over five years to outbreak reports from laboratories and local health units. Four percent of alerts corresponded to a confirmed outbreak or cluster within 14 days. Most false alerts arose from reporting artefacts, duplicate records and changes in emergency department coding. Gastrointestinal alerts in people aged 65 and over had the highest predictive value, often linked to care homes. The authors suggest that validation should concentrate on excluding artefacts quickly and on alerts in settings with vulnerable populations.

records.title: Validation practices for syndromic surveillance signals: a survey of 62 public health agencies
records.authors: Haddad-Lindgren S, Mwale-Oduya P, Ferreira-Hart K
records.abstract: We surveyed 62 public health agencies about how syndromic surveillance alerts are validated. Seventy-one percent had no written validation procedure. The median reported time per alert was 45 minutes, with a range from under 10 minutes to more than three hours, and agencies rarely measured how often real events were dismissed. Agencies with a written procedure reported more consistent escalation decisions but not shorter times. Respondents identified duplicate records and coding changes as the commonest causes of false alerts and staff shortages at weekends as the commonest cause of delay.

records.title: Panel review as a reference standard for outbreak signals: agreement and hindsight bias
records.abstract: We asked panels of three epidemiologists to classify 300 past syndromic alerts as true or false signals, first without and then with knowledge of later outbreak reports. Agreement between panels without outcome knowledge was moderate (kappa 0.52). With outcome knowledge, panels reclassified 18 percent of alerts, almost always towards the known outcome. Disagreement was greatest for small gastrointestinal clusters in older adults. The authors conclude that panel review is a weak reference standard for estimating the accuracy of validation procedures and that outcome-blinded panels still disagree substantially.

records.title: Checklist-based alert triage in a national surveillance centre: internal evaluation summary
records.abstract: This summary describes the introduction of a checklist for triaging syndromic surveillance alerts in a national surveillance centre. Staff reported that the checklist made handovers easier and that decisions were easier to explain to managers. The summary states that validation became faster and that no outbreaks were missed, but it gives no figures for time, no definition of a missed outbreak and no comparison period. It lists the checklist items, which resemble those of other agencies. The summary carries no date, and the evaluation period and the number of alerts are not reported.

records.title: Randomising days rather than alerts: contamination and learning effects in trials of surveillance procedures
records.abstract: Trials that randomise individual alerts to a new validation procedure risk contamination, because the same staff handle both arms on the same day and carry the new procedure over. Using simulation based on two completed evaluations, we compared individual alert randomisation with randomisation of duty days. Day randomisation reduced contamination because staff used only one procedure on a given day, at the cost of a modest design effect when alerts on the same day are correlated. With about five alerts a day and an intracluster correlation near 0.1, the design effect was about 1.4.

records.title: Syndromic surveillance signal validation: report of a regional workshop
records.abstract: This report summarises a one-day workshop of epidemiologists from several regional agencies on validating syndromic surveillance signals. Participants agreed that a shared checklist would be useful and listed checks for duplicates, reporting artefacts, age and place clustering and laboratory confirmation. Participants disagreed on whether signals from small rural emergency departments should be escalated more readily, given small counts. The report records opinions only, gives no data on the performance of any procedure, and carries no date or list of participating agencies.

records.title: Time to public health action after syndromic alerts for norovirus in long-term care: a case series
records.abstract: We reviewed 11 norovirus clusters in long-term care homes that were preceded by a syndromic surveillance alert. In 5 of the 11 clusters, public health action followed the first alert by two days or more, usually because the first alert was dismissed as an artefact. Clusters with action within one day of the first alert had fewer cases on average, although the homes also differed in size and staffing. The authors recommend that gastrointestinal alerts involving older adults in a small area are never dismissed without checking for care homes.

response.synthesis: Eight retrieved records; six appraised at abstract level and two undated grey records left unrated. A randomised comparison showed a structured protocol halving time to a validation decision, with contamination between arms; a simulation study shows that randomising duty days limits contamination at a small design effect. Panel review is a weak reference standard because panels disagree and hindsight shifts their judgement, which undermines an accuracy study. Only about four percent of alerts are real, so missed events will be few, and care home clusters show the cost of dismissal. The two undated records report opinions and unquantified claims.
response.gradeRationale: One randomised comparison and consistent methods evidence support the time outcome and the design choice; missed events rest on case series. Moderate certainty that structured validation can shorten decisions; low certainty about missed events.
response.summary: Eight retrieved records; six appraised, two undated records not rated; five claims recorded; overall certainty moderate.

response.reading: The checklist acts on the epidemiologist's process, not on the signal, so its value lies in faster and more consistent decisions without more dismissed true events. An accuracy framing needs a reference standard that hindsight corrupts. A randomised comparison of procedures measures time directly, but contamination between arms is likely when the same people validate both, which day-level randomisation addresses. True events are rare, so missed events need case-by-case review rather than a test.

response.designSummary: Randomised comparison with duty days as clusters; alerts analysed individually with day as a random effect.
response.sampleSize: About 890 alerts over six months, about 445 per arm, with about five alerts a day. Time to decision is right-skewed; on the log scale with a standard deviation near 0.9 and an intracluster correlation near 0.1 (design effect about 1.4, claim c3), the effective sample is about 318 alerts per arm, giving 80 percent power at two-sided alpha 0.05 to detect a ratio of median times of about 0.82, an 18 percent reduction. About 4 percent of alerts are real (claim c4), so each arm will see about 18 true events, too few for a statistical comparison of missed events.
response.primaryAnalysis: Linear mixed model of log time to decision with procedure, syndrome and weekday as fixed effects and duty day as a random intercept; the result is reported as a ratio of geometric mean times with its 95 percent confidence interval.
response.secondaryAnalysis: Escalations per 100 alerts by procedure with a mixed logistic model; dismissed true events listed and reviewed individually; contamination reported monthly.
response.missingData: Alerts without a recorded decision time are counted and reported; the primary analysis excludes them, with a sensitivity analysis assigning them the 95th percentile time of their arm.
response.multiplicity: One primary outcome; secondary outcomes reported with confidence intervals only.
response.software: R with lme4; allocation list and analysis code held by the analyst outside the rota.
overfittingGuards: Two adjustment variables fixed in advance
Safety review criteria fixed before the first study day
response.summary: About 445 alerts per arm; 80 percent power for an 18 percent shorter decision time; missed events reviewed case by case.

response.risks: The main risk is to the public: a true event dismissed on a checklist or usual day. The safety panel reviews each dismissed true event within a week and can stop the evaluation.
response.consent: No personal information is used beyond line lists already handled in routine surveillance; the six epidemiologists are informed and agree to the allocation of their duty days; individual consent is not required for program evaluation under the chair's classification.
response.data: Only alert identifiers, time stamps, syndrome, decision and outbreak linkage are extracted; data stay in the agency's surveillance environment.
response.equity: PROGRESS-Plus: people in care homes and in small rural communities generate small-count signals that are easiest to dismiss. The checklist includes an explicit care home and small-area check, and dismissals are reported by setting and by rural or urban area.
response.effectiveness: The evaluation shows whether the checklist saves epidemiologist time without harming detection, which decides whether it becomes standard.
response.efficiency: Uses existing staff and logs; configuration change only.
response.costs: Analyst time for allocation and analysis within existing roles.
response.partnerships: Local health units (outbreak confirmation), the laboratory network (reports), and a care home sector representative on the safety panel.
response.rebPath: Classified by the research ethics committee chair as program evaluation not requiring review (letter REC-2026-PE-07, 2026-09-10); the director approved the evaluation (memo PHA-DIR-2026-31).
response.limitations: Six epidemiologists in one agency; contamination may persist; missed events too few to compare.
response.summary: Program evaluation with a safety panel, staff agreement, and equity reporting for care homes and rural areas.

response.title: Structured validation of syndromic surveillance alerts: a day-randomised comparison in a regional public health agency
response.abstract: Objective: to test whether a structured validation checklist shortens the time from syndromic surveillance alert to validation decision without increasing dismissed true events. Design: randomised comparison with duty days allocated to the checklist or usual validation, January to June 2027. Primary outcome: time to validation decision. Results and conclusions will be written after the evaluation.
response.introduction: Syndromic surveillance generates many alerts, few of them real, and validation practice varies widely. Accuracy studies of validation procedures depend on panel review, which hindsight biases.
response.methods: Duty days were randomised in blocks within month. Time stamps came from the surveillance log, and outbreak reports classified alerts. A mixed model compared log times; a safety panel reviewed every dismissed true event.
response.results: No data have been collected yet. The report will present alert flow, times by procedure, escalations, contamination and each dismissed true event.
response.discussion: The discussion will weigh time saved against dismissed events and state whether the checklist should become standard.
response.limitations: One agency; six epidemiologists; few true events.
response.conclusion: To be written after the evaluation; it will not claim a change in outbreak detection rates.

store.title: Structured validation of syndromic surveillance alerts in a regional public health agency

includes: Structured validation of syndromic surveillance alerts in a regional public health agency

steps.note: recommendedFamily, selectionStatus and actionStatus require S11; the claims S13. One click gives one file (G10).

path.problem.rawNeed:
I am a surveillance epidemiologist at a regional public health agency serving about 2.4 million people. Our syndromic surveillance system scans emergency department chief complaints and pharmacy sales every morning and generates about 35 statistical alerts a week for respiratory, gastrointestinal and rash syndromes. Each alert is validated by the epidemiologist on duty, who looks at line lists, calls hospitals if needed and decides whether to escalate. We have no written procedure: some of us spend two hours on an alert and others dismiss it in five minutes, and last winter a norovirus cluster in two care homes was dismissed twice before the third alert was escalated.

We have drafted a structured validation checklist with fixed data checks (duplicate records, reporting artefacts, clustering by age and place, comparison with laboratory reports) and a rule for when to escalate. I am not sure how to evaluate it. One option is to treat it like a test and estimate its sensitivity and specificity against a panel review of past alerts. Another is to randomise incoming alerts, or duty days, to the checklist or to usual validation for six months and compare the time to a validation decision and the events that were missed. My director wants to know whether the checklist makes validation faster without missing real events before it becomes standard procedure.

Six epidemiologists share the duty rota and we cannot hire. Alerts and decisions are logged in our surveillance database with time stamps, and outbreak reports from laboratories and local health units tell us later which alerts were real. The chair of the agency's research ethics committee has confirmed that an evaluation of an internal procedure that uses no personal information counts as program evaluation.
